little.skill: Tell a grown-up, call for help
little.twist: The helper on the phone also asks where you are.
little.can_now: tell a grown-up when someone is poorly or hurt, help a hot friend into the shade, and call {number} on a phone when no grown-up is near

steps.say: The practice playground. Sometimes someone suddenly feels poorly. Little helpers can help in two ways: tell a grown-up, and call for help.
Lulu bumped her head on the slide. She says she's fine. What do you do? Touch Gus to tell him.
steps.done: Tell a grown-up about every bump on the head, even a small one.

steps.say: Bobo has a nosebleed.

choices.text: Help him sit, lean forward, and tell a grown-up

choices.why: Lean forward, not back. And tell a grown-up.

steps.done: Sitting, leaning forward: a grown-up pinches his nose.

steps.say: It's a very hot day. Pip-pop feels hot and dizzy. Help her into the shade.
steps.done: In the shade, out of the sun.

steps.say: Give her some water to sip.
steps.done: Little sips. And tell a grown-up too.

steps.say: Mo ate a biscuit and now her lips are swelling up.

choices.why: Swelling lips can be an allergy: tell a grown-up straight away.

steps.done: Straight away: a grown-up knows what to do.

steps.say: If no grown-up is near, you can call for help on a phone. Let's practise on the play phone.
Pick up the phone.
steps.done: Phone in your hand.

steps.say: Press {number}: {number_words}.
steps.done: Calling...

steps.say: The helper asks: what happened?

choices.why: Tell the helper what happened to your friend.

steps.done: The helper is listening.

steps.say: The helper asks: where are you?

choices.text: At the picnic place in the park

choices.why: Look around: say the place's name, or what you can see.

steps.done: Now the helpers know where to come.

steps.say: The helper says: help is on its way. Stay with your friend.
You did it! Tell a grown-up, help a friend into the shade, and call {number} if no grown-up is near.

check.say: Your friend bumped their head. You...
A friend feels hot and dizzy in the sun. Help them...
No grown-up is near and your friend is very poorly. You call...

name_it.title: Tell, help, call
lines: Someone is poorly or hurt: tell a grown-up.
A bump on the head: always tell a grown-up.
Too hot: into the shade, with sips of water.
No grown-up near: call {number}, say what happened and where.
name_it.source: The British Red Cross (first aid for children), St John Ambulance and the NHS

little.try_real: With a grown-up, practise what you would say on the phone: what happened, and where you are. Never call {number} for real unless it's a real emergency.

sources.fact: Children can help by telling an adult and calling the emergency number if no adult is there, saying what happened and where.
sources.source: British Red Cross, first aid for children

sources.fact: Tell an adult about any bump on the head; watch for being sick, sleepy, confused or a bad headache.
Heat exhaustion: move to a cool place, give water to drink, cool the skin; call for help if they don't get better.

middle.twist: Nothing glows: Bobo's nosebleed, the inhaler's order and the heat are all up to you.
middle.can_now: help with a nosebleed, a bump on the head, an asthma attack with an inhaler and spacer, and too much heat

steps.say: The practice room. Today: a nosebleed, a bump on the head, an inhaler with a spacer, and too much sun. This is practice. A real first aid course teaches more.

safe_mistake.wrong: tipping the head back for a nosebleed
safe_mistake.why: Tipping the head back makes it run down the throat, which can make you cough and feel sick.
safe_mistake.right: Sit, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of the nose.

steps.say: Bobo has a nosebleed. Help him sit the right way.
steps.done: Sitting, leaning forward.

safe_mistake.wrong: tipping the head back for a nosebleed
safe_mistake.why: Tipping the head back makes it run down the throat, which can make you cough and feel sick.
safe_mistake.right: Sit, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of the nose.

steps.say: Bobo has a nosebleed. How does he sit?
steps.done: Leaning forward: you knew by yourself.

steps.say: Pinch the soft part of his nose, just below the bony bit.
steps.done: Pinch, and keep pinching.

steps.label: 10 minutes
steps.say: Keep pinching for 10 minutes, breathing through the mouth. Let's speed up the clock.
steps.done: Ten minutes: it has stopped.

steps.say: If a nosebleed goes on for longer than 10 to 15 minutes...

choices.text: A grown-up takes them to get help

choices.why: A nosebleed that won't stop needs a doctor's help: tell a grown-up.

steps.done: A grown-up gets help.

steps.say: At the playground Lulu bumps her head, then says she's fine.

choices.text: Tell a grown-up, who keeps an eye on her

choices.why: Always tell a grown-up about a bump on the head: they watch for a headache, sleepiness or being sick.

steps.done: A grown-up watches her for the rest of the day.

steps.say: Kiki has asthma. She's coughing and wheezing: she needs her reliever inhaler, the blue one, with its spacer. Stay calm.
First help Kiki sit up straight.
steps.done: Sitting up helps her breathe.

steps.say: Kiki uses her own inhaler, the way her asthma plan says. You can practise how with a trainer: it has no medicine in it.
Take the cap off and shake the inhaler.
steps.done: Shaken.

steps.say: Put it into the end of the spacer.
steps.done: In.

steps.say: Breathe out gently, lips round the mouthpiece, then press the inhaler down once.
steps.done: One press: the medicine goes into the spacer.

steps.say: Breathe out, lips round the mouthpiece. Now what?
steps.done: One press, by yourself.

steps.say: Now breathe in and out slowly through the spacer, five times.
steps.done: Slow and calm. Not getting better? Tell a grown-up and call {number}.

steps.say: A very hot day. Pip-pop feels dizzy and hot, with a headache. Help her into the shade.
steps.done: Shade first.

steps.say: Help her cool down: sips of cool water.
steps.done: Sips of water, and cool cloths on her skin.

steps.say: She's still very hot, and now she's muddled and not getting better.

choices.text: Let her play in the sun
choices.why: Heatstroke is an emergency: call {number}, and keep cooling her.

steps.done: Help is coming. Keep cooling her in the shade.

steps.say: Lean forward and pinch, tell a grown-up about bumps, the inhaler with its spacer, and shade, water and {number} for heat.

check.say: An inhaler with a spacer: after one press you...
A bump on the head. You...
Someone is hot, dizzy and muddled. You...

name_it.title: Lean forward, puff, shade
lines: A nosebleed: sit, lean forward, pinch the soft part for 10 minutes.
A bump on the head: always tell a grown-up.
Asthma: sit up, their own inhaler and spacer: shake, press once, breathe slowly.
Too hot: shade, cool, water; muddled and no better: call {number}.
name_it.source: The NHS, St John Ambulance and the British Red Cross, and Asthma + Lung UK

middle.try_real: Ask a grown-up to show you where your family keeps its first aid kit. If someone you know has asthma, ask them to show you their spacer.

sources.fact: Nosebleed: sit down, lean forward, pinch the soft part of the nose just above the nostrils for 10 to 15 minutes, breathe through the mouth; don't tip the head back.
Get medical help if a nosebleed lasts longer than 10 to 15 minutes.
Using an inhaler with a spacer: shake, fit it into the spacer, breathe out, seal the lips round the mouthpiece, press once, then breathe slowly in and out (about five breaths).
sources.source: Asthma + Lung UK, using a spacer with tidal breathing

sources.fact: During an asthma attack: sit up straight, take the reliever inhaler as the asthma action plan says, and call 999 or 112 if it isn't getting better.
Heat exhaustion: move to a cool place, drink water, cool the skin; heatstroke (no better after 30 minutes, confused, not sweating) is an emergency: call 999 or 112.
Tell an adult about any head injury and watch for symptoms such as being sick, a headache that won't go, or drowsiness.

big.twist: Nothing glows: the signs, the cushion and when to call are up to you.
big.can_now: spot anaphylaxis and call for help, know how an auto-injector works (practised on a trainer), and keep someone safe during a seizure and in the recovery position after

steps.say: Practice for older helpers: an allergy emergency and the auto-injector trainer pen, then how to help someone having a seizure. This is practice. A real first aid course teaches more.

lines.sign_breath: Breathing that is noisy or hard.

steps.say: Mo ate a biscuit with nuts in it, and she is allergic to nuts. Find the signs.
steps.done: These signs can mean anaphylaxis: a serious allergy emergency.

lines.sign_breath: Breathing that is noisy or hard.

steps.say: Mo ate something with nuts in it. Find the three signs of an allergy emergency.
steps.done: All three, by yourself: anaphylaxis.

steps.say: What first?

choices.text: Shout for a grown-up and call {number}: say 'anaphylaxis'
Wait to see if it gets better
choices.why: Anaphylaxis can get worse fast: help now.

steps.done: Gus comes running, and the ambulance is on its way.

steps.say: Mo carries her own auto-injector pen. A real pen is only ever the person's own, prescribed for them: a grown-up, or Mo herself, uses it. Now practise with a trainer: no needle, no medicine.
Hold the trainer in your fist, orange end down. Pull off the blue cap: blue to the sky.
steps.done: Blue to the sky.

steps.say: Orange to the thigh: push it firmly against the outside of the practice pad's thigh until it clicks, and hold it there.
steps.done: Click, and held. A real pen's instructions say how long to hold it.

steps.say: Gus used Mo's pen and the ambulance is coming. Now?

choices.text: Lie her down with her legs raised, or sitting up if breathing is hard

choices.why: Lie her down with her legs raised, or sit her up if breathing is hard. Don't let her stand or walk.

steps.done: Lying down, legs up, and someone stays with her.

steps.say: Practice time. Bobo the buddy pretends to have a seizure: he's on the floor, his body jerking, and he can't answer. Stay calm.
Time it: start the stopwatch.
steps.done: The clock is running.

steps.say: Move hard things away from him.
steps.done: Space all round him.

safe_mistake.wrong: putting something in someone's mouth during a seizure
safe_mistake.why: Nothing goes in the mouth: it can hurt their teeth or block the air, and nobody can swallow their tongue.
safe_mistake.right: Something soft under the head, and nothing in the mouth.

steps.say: What helps him now?
steps.done: Something soft under his head.

safe_mistake.wrong: putting something in someone's mouth during a seizure
safe_mistake.why: Nothing goes in the mouth: it can hurt their teeth or block the air, and nobody can swallow their tongue.
safe_mistake.right: Something soft under the head, and nothing in the mouth.

steps.say: What goes under his head?
steps.done: Soft, under his head, and nothing in his mouth.

steps.say: Do you hold him still?

choices.text: Yes, hold his arms and legs
choices.why: Holding someone down can hurt them, and it won't stop the seizure. Keep them safe and wait.

steps.done: Stay beside him, talk calmly, and watch the clock.

steps.say: The jerking stops after 2 minutes. He's breathing, but sleepy. Now the recovery position.
Move his arm nearest you out, like the letter L.
steps.done: Arm out.

steps.say: Put his other hand against his cheek.
steps.done: Hand to cheek.

steps.say: Bend his far knee up.
steps.done: Knee up.

steps.say: Pull the knee towards you, and he rolls onto his side.
steps.done: On his side: his airway stays clear.

steps.say: When do you call {number} for a seizure?

choices.text: Over 5 minutes, a first seizure, or they're hurt

choices.why: Call {number} if it lasts more than 5 minutes, it's their first, they're hurt, or they don't wake up properly.

steps.done: And stay with him until he is fully awake.

steps.say: Spot anaphylaxis and call {number}; blue to the sky, orange to the thigh; and for a seizure: time it, clear the space, soft under the head, nothing in the mouth, never hold down, then the recovery position.

An auto-injector pen: blue to the sky, orange to...
You call {number} if a seizure lasts more than...

name_it.title: Pen, call, keep them safe
lines: Anaphylaxis: swelling, a rash, noisy breathing: call {number} and say 'anaphylaxis'.
Their own pen: blue to the sky, orange to the thigh; then lie them down, legs up.
A seizure: time it, move hard things away, soft under the head.
Nothing in the mouth, never hold them down; after: the recovery position. Over 5 minutes: call {number}.
name_it.source: Anaphylaxis UK and the NHS, Epilepsy Action and the Epilepsy Foundation, and St John Ambulance

big.try_real: If someone in your family or class has an auto-injector, ask a grown-up to show you their trainer pen. Learn the seizure steps together from Epilepsy Action's poster.

sources.fact: Anaphylaxis signs: swelling of the throat, tongue or face, breathing difficulty, a rash; call 999 or 112 and say it's anaphylaxis; use their adrenaline auto-injector if they have one.
EpiPen: 'blue to the sky, orange to the thigh': remove the blue safety cap, push the orange tip into the outer thigh until it clicks, and hold.
sources.source: The EpiPen manufacturer's instructions; Anaphylaxis UK, how to use adrenaline auto-injectors

sources.fact: After the auto-injector: lie the person down with legs raised; if breathing is difficult, sit them up; don't let them stand or walk.

Seizure first aid: time it, move hard objects away, cushion the head; don't restrain them or put anything in their mouth; afterwards, the recovery position; call 999 or 112 if it lasts more than 5 minutes.
Stay with the person until they are fully aware; never put anything in the mouth; call an ambulance for a first seizure or one over 5 minutes.
